data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["Biological evolution has no conscious goal of testing; Popperian science explicitly aims at falsification.","Legal systems aim for a verdict (truth-equivalent); Popperian science aims for endless conjecture and refutation without final verdicts."],"overturn_conditions":["If biological fitness is shown to be predictive of future survival in a way that transcends mere description, the analogy might support induction.","If the legal system is shown to rely on probabilistic guilt rather than adversarial stress-testing, the structural parallel fails."],"shared_structure":["Selection of the 'fittest' entity based on survival of past challenges.","No guarantee of future survival or absolute truth, only relative robustness.","Process driven by elimination of weak candidates rather than verification of strong ones."],"source_memory_refs":["evolutionary_biology_natural_selection","legal_adversarial_system"],"transfer_claims":["Just as we bet on the organism that survived diverse environments without assuming it will survive the next one, we bet on the corroborated theory without assuming it will pass the next test.","The 'fitness' is retrospective, not predictive."]},"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms not as an inductive inference that the future will resemble the past, but as a non-inductive methodological rule to maximize the severity of future tests; however, accepting this defense costs us the ability to claim that such preferences make the theory more likely to be true or successful in application, reducing the preference to a strategic gamble rather than a rational expectation of utility.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the preference implies any expectation that the theory will work in practical applications (e.g., engineering bridges), it smuggles in induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If Popper's rejection of verisimilitude (due to logical incoherence) stands, there is no objective metric to rank theories other than falsification status, making the preference arbitrary.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 'metaphysical faith' in the uniformity of nature is required to act on any theory, then the distinction between corroboration and probability collapses in practice.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism distinguishes between 'inductive justification' (claiming past success increases future probability) and 'methodological selection' (choosing the theory that offers the best chance of being falsified if false). By preferring the most severely tested theory, scientists select the one with the highest empirical content and the greatest exposure to potential refutation. If it survives again, we learn more; if it fails, we eliminate a strong contender. This avoids induction because it does not assume the surviving theory will continue to survive, only that it is currently the most informative target for criticism.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
